Management: Tocolytic agents and steroids are used in management of pregnancies with preterm labor between 24 and 34 weeks' gestation or EFW 600-2500 g. Once a pregnancy has continued beyond 34-37 weeks' EGA or EFW greater than 2500 g, the fetal survival rate is within 1% of the survival rate at 37 weeks. Fetal morbidity is less severe and is rarely a cause of long-term sequelae. Fuhermore, corticosteroids have not been shown to be of benefit in fetuses of this age or size. Therefore, expectant management is usually the recommended course of action

Signs and symptoms: The typical symptoms of malignant hyperthermia are due to a hypercatabolic state, which presents as a very high temperature, an increased heart rate and breathing rate, increased carbon dioxide production, increased oxygen consumption, acidosis, rigid muscles, and rhabdomyolysis. The symptoms usually develop within one hour after exposure to trigger substances, but may even occur several hours later in rare instances. Causes: Volatile anesthetic gases halothane, sevoflurane, desflurane Local anesthetics lidocaine, bupivicaine, mepivacaine Depolarizing muscle succinylcholine relaxants Other Opiates (morphine, fentanyl), ketamine, barbiturates, nitrous oxide, propofol, etomidate, benzodiazepines Genetics: Malignant hyperthermia's inheritance is autosomal dominant. The defect is typically located on the long arm of the nineteenth chromosome (19q13.1) involving the ryanodine receptor.

items.q: Apatient who is at risk of estrogen dependent carcinoma and hence estrogen is contraindicated. So in order to prevent vasomotor symptoms, which drug is given?
items.exp: Clonidine REF: Novak's gynecology 13th edition page 455 In women for whom hormone replacement is contraindicated, multiple alternative treatments for hot flashes have been developed. Somewhat effective alternatives may be progestins such as medroxyprogesterone (10 to 30 mg daily orally) or megestrol acetate (20 to 40 mg daily orally). If either of these progestins results in intolerable side effects, the use of alternative progestins may be considered, although few data exist regarding their efficacy. In addition to the progestins, other nonsteroidal treatments for hot flashes have been developed. One of the best studied is the b 2-adrenergic agonist, clonidine. This drug probably works through both central and peripheral mechanisms and can be given either orally (0.05 mg twice daily) or by transdermal patch.

items.q: Which arterial segment is the most common anatomical site for saccular (berry) intracranial aneurysms?
items.exp: The anterior communicating artery junction is the most frequent site of intracranial berry aneurysms, accounting for approximately 30-35% of all cases.
r: Correct. Anterior communicating artery is the most common berry aneurysm location.
Incorrect. Basilar bifurcation accounts for approximately 5-10% of aneurysms.
Incorrect. MCA bifurcation accounts for about 20-25%.
Incorrect. PICA aneurysms are less frequent.
items.kp: The anterior communicating artery junction is the most common site of intracranial saccular berry aneurysms.

items.q: The conversion of the normal cellular prion protein (PrPC) into the infectious scrapie isoform (PrPSc) in Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease involves which primary conformational change?
o: Transition from alpha-helices to abundant beta-pleated sheets
Cleavage of the amino-terminal signal peptide
items.exp: PrPC has 42% alpha-helix content and little beta-sheet. PrPSc shifts to 43% beta-sheet and reduced alpha-helix, rendering it insoluble, protease-resistant, and self-templating.
r: Correct. Prion conversion involves refolding from alpha-helices into beta-sheets.
Incorrect. The primary sequence is unchanged; no unique peptide cleavage occurs.
Incorrect. Prion disease is a conformational shift, not hyperphosphorylation.
Incorrect. Disulfide bonds remain intact.
items.kp: Prion diseases arise from conformational refolding of normal alpha-helical PrPC into protease-resistant beta-sheet rich PrPSc.

items.q: A 40-year-old woman is diagnosed with mild pityriasis versicolor affecting her upper back. What is the recommended first-line topical treatment?
o: Topical ketoconazole shampoo (or selenium sulfide shampoo)
items.exp: First-line therapy for localized pityriasis versicolor is topical antifungal shampoo, such as ketoconazole 2% shampoo or selenium sulfide, applied to affected areas and left on for several minutes before washing off, used daily or several times weekly for 2-4 weeks. Oral terbinafine is ineffective for Malassezia.
r: Correct: Topical ketoconazole or selenium sulfide shampoo is first-line for pityriasis versicolor.
Oral terbinafine does not reach therapeutic concentrations in sebum and is ineffective against Malassezia.
Topical steroids promote yeast growth and worsen fungal infections.
Aciclovir is an antiviral for herpesviruses and has no antifungal activity.
items.kp: Topical ketoconazole or selenium sulfide shampoo is first-line for pityriasis versicolor; oral terbinafine is ineffective.

items.q: A 42-year-old woman presents with eight weeks of symmetric pain and swelling in her metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints, with two hours of morning stiffness. Which investigation offers the highest specificity for rheumatoid arthritis?
items.exp: Anti-CCP antibodies exhibit high specificity (>95%) for rheumatoid arthritis and predict erosive disease. Rheumatoid factor has lower specificity and is positive in other connective tissue diseases and chronic infections.
r: Correct: Anti-CCP antibodies provide superior specificity (>95%) for rheumatoid arthritis.
Rheumatoid factor is sensitive but less specific, appearing in Sjogren syndrome, SLE and chronic infections.
ESR is a non-specific inflammatory marker.
ANA is sensitive for SLE but non-specific for rheumatoid arthritis.
items.kp: Anti-CCP has superior specificity over rheumatoid factor for rheumatoid arthritis.

items.q: Which medical therapy provides the greatest reduction in menstrual blood loss for women with idiopathic heavy menstrual bleeding?
o: Cyclic oral medroxyprogesterone acetate for 10 days/month
items.exp: The 52 mg LNG-IUS is the most effective medical treatment for heavy menstrual bleeding, reducing measured menstrual blood loss by 70% to 95% within 6 to 12 months. Short-course luteal progestins (10 days/month) are ineffective for HMB.
r: Correct. The 52 mg LNG-IUS achieves up to 90-95% reduction in menstrual blood loss, superior to all oral regimens.
Incorrect. Tranexamic acid achieves a 40-55% reduction.
Incorrect. Cyclic 10-day progestins do not reliably reduce blood loss and are not recommended for HMB.
Incorrect. NSAIDs achieve approximately 25-35% reduction.
items.kp: The 52 mg LNG-IUS is the most effective medical therapy for heavy menstrual bleeding, reducing blood loss by up to 95%.

items.q: A 34-year-old man with chronic OCD achieves complete remission of his symptoms after 6 months of treatment with oral fluoxetine 60 mg daily. In accordance with NICE guideline CG31, what is the recommended duration of continuation therapy with the effective dose to prevent relapse?
o: Continue for at least 12 months after remission
Discontinue immediately once remission is achieved
Taper off over 2 weeks following remission
Continue for a maximum of 3 months then switch to psychotherapy
items.exp: NICE guideline CG31 recommends that patients with OCD who respond to medication should continue treatment for at least 12 months after achieving remission. Discontinuing medication earlier carries a relapse rate of 60-80%. Tapering should be gradual when eventual discontinuation is attempted.
r: Correct: Pharmacotherapy should be continued for at least 12 months post-remission to prevent relapse.
Immediate discontinuation carries an unacceptable 60-80% relapse risk.
Tapering after 2 weeks is premature and leads to rapid relapse.
A 3-month total course is insufficient for maintenance in OCD.
items.kp: Successful pharmacotherapy in OCD should be continued for at least 12 months after remission to prevent relapse.

items.q: In the physiological timeline of surgical wound healing, at what postoperative interval does wound tensile strength reach approximately 20% of unwounded baseline skin?
items.exp: Wound tensile strength develops slowly. It is virtually negligible during the first 48 hours, rises to approximately 3% at 1 week, reaches about 20% at 3 weeks (the transition from proliferative to remodeling phase), and plateaus at a maximum of 70% to 80% of original unwounded skin strength by 1 year.
r: Incorrect. Tensile strength is nearly zero during the initial inflammatory phase.
Incorrect. At 7 days tensile strength is only ~3-5% (sutures provide primary support).
Correct. At 3 weeks tensile strength reaches ~20%, allowing safe skin suture removal.
Incorrect. At 1 year tensile strength reaches its plateau of ~80%.
items.kp: Wound tensile strength reaches 20% at 3 weeks and plateaus at ~80% at 1 year.

items.q: What is the most frequent anatomical position of the vermiform appendix in the human population?
items.exp: The retrocecal and retrocolic position is the most common anatomical location of the appendix, accounting for approximately 65% of cases.
r: Correct. Retrocecal position accounts for roughly 65% of normal anatomical variations.
Incorrect. Pelvic position accounts for approximately 30%.
Incorrect. Subcecal is uncommon (2%).
Incorrect. Pre-ileal is rare (1%).
items.kp: The retrocecal position is the most common anatomical orientation of the vermiform appendix (65%).

items.q: What is the most common pathogenic mutation in the CFTR gene responsible for cystic fibrosis, and what class of processing defect does it cause?
o: F508del (deletion of phenylalanine at position 508), causing Class II protein misfolding and ERAD degradation
G542X nonsense mutation, causing Class I absent protein synthesis
G551D missense mutation, causing Class III defective channel gating
R117H missense mutation, causing Class IV reduced channel conductance
items.exp: F508del is present in ~70% of CF alleles. The three-base-pair deletion of phenylalanine-508 prevents proper CFTR protein folding in the ER, routing it to ERAD proteasomal degradation so zero channel reaches the apical membrane.
r: Correct. F508del causes misfolding and premature ERAD proteasomal destruction (Class II).
Incorrect. G542X is a Class I stop codon mutation.
Incorrect. G551D is a Class III gating mutation treated with ivacaftor.
Incorrect. R117H is a Class IV conductance defect.
items.kp: CFTR F508del is a Class II mutation: the misfolded channel is caught by ER quality control and degraded by ERAD before reaching the cell surface.

items.q: A 22-year-old athlete presents with itchy, peeling, macerated skin between his toes, particularly in the fourth interdigital web space. Examination reveals white macerated fissured epidermis. What is the diagnosis and appropriate initial treatment?
o: Tinea pedis (athlete's foot); treated with topical terbinafine 1% cream
Contact dermatitis; treated with topical calcineurin inhibitors
Pitted keratolysis; treated with topical erythromycin
items.exp: Tinea pedis (athlete's foot) is the most common dermatophyte infection, commonly presenting with interdigital scaling, maceration and pruritus in the 4th web space. First-line therapy is a topical antifungal cream (e.g. topical terbinafine 1% applied once or twice daily for 1-2 weeks).
r: Correct: Interdigital maceration is tinea pedis, treated first-line with topical terbinafine.
Oral steroids are contraindicated for fungal infections and cause severe exacerbation.
Contact dermatitis does not present with isolated macerated toe web fissures.
Pitted keratolysis produces punch-out pits and malodour, driven by bacterial infection.
items.kp: Interdigital tinea pedis presents with toe web maceration, treated with topical antifungal cream.

items.q: A 60-year-old woman with long-standing erosive rheumatoid arthritis is scheduled for elective total hip replacement under general anaesthesia. Which preoperative investigation is critical to ensure anaesthetic airway safety?
o: Flexion and extension cervical spine radiographs to assess atlantoaxial subluxation
items.exp: Cervical spine involvement occurs in up to 30-50% of chronic rheumatoid arthritis patients, particularly atlantoaxial subluxation. Flexion and extension lateral radiographs assess the anterior atlantodental interval; unrecognised instability risks spinal cord transection during endotracheal intubation.
r: Correct: Cervical spine flexion and extension radiographs assess atlantoaxial stability before intubation.
Coronary CT is not routine without cardiac symptoms.
Echocardiography evaluates cardiac function but does not detect cervical spine instability.
Spirometry does not address the acute mechanical risk of spinal cord compression.
items.kp: Assess cervical spine flexion and extension in long-standing RA prior to general anaesthesia.

items.q: A 52-year-old postmenopausal woman with obesity presents with a single episode of vaginal spotting. Transvaginal ultrasound demonstrates an endometrial thickness of 8 mm. What is the definitive management step?
items.exp: Postmenopausal bleeding requires prompt histological evaluation. An endometrial thickness > 4 mm on transvaginal ultrasound in a postmenopausal patient carries an elevated risk of endometrial cancer (~10%) and mandates outpatient endometrial biopsy.
r: Correct. Postmenopausal bleeding with endometrial stripe > 4 mm mandates histological sampling.
Incorrect. Reassurance is dangerous because postmenopausal bleeding carries a 10% risk of carcinoma.
Incorrect. Estrogen is contraindicated in uninvestigated vaginal bleeding.
Incorrect. Hormonal therapy without histological diagnosis is malpractice.
items.kp: Postmenopausal bleeding with endometrial thickness > 4 mm on ultrasound requires mandatory endometrial biopsy.

items.q: A 22-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder is being considered for maintenance therapy. Her psychiatrist notes that sodium valproate is strictly contraindicated in girls and women of childbearing potential unless conditions of a Pregnancy Prevention Programme are met. What are the major risks of in utero sodium valproate exposure?
o: High rate of major congenital malformations (10%, including neural tube defects) and neurodevelopmental delay (30-40%)
Isolated neonatal hypoglycaemia without physical malformations
Transient maternal alopecia without fetal effect
items.exp: Sodium valproate is profoundly teratogenic. In utero exposure causes a 10% rate of major congenital malformations (neural tube defects, craniofacial defects, cardiac malformations, hypospadias) and a 30-40% incidence of long-term neurodevelopmental disorders, cognitive impairment, and autism spectrum disorders. MHRA and NICE strictly restrict its use in women of childbearing potential.
r: Correct: Valproate causes 10% major malformations (neural tube defects) and 30-40% neurodevelopmental disability.
Valproate risks are far more severe than isolated neonatal hypoglycaemia.
Valproate causes severe permanent structural and developmental damage, not mild jitteriness.
Fetal risks are devastating and permanent, not limited to maternal alopecia.
items.kp: Sodium valproate in pregnancy causes a 10% rate of major malformations and a 30-40% risk of neurodevelopmental disorders.

items.q: A 28-year-old polytrauma patient following a high-speed vehicular collision presents with a heart rate of 128 bpm, blood pressure of 86/60 mmHg, respiratory rate of 32/min, cold pale extremities, and confusion. According to the ATLS classification, what class of hemorrhagic shock does this represent?
items.exp: Class III hemorrhagic shock represents 30% to 40% blood volume loss (1500 to 2000 mL in a 70 kg adult). It is defined by marked tachycardia (>120 bpm), overt hypotension, tachypnea (30-40/min), oliguria, and mental confusion. Class II features normal systolic pressure with narrowed pulse pressure; Class IV features severe hypotension and coma.
r: Incorrect. Class I features normal vitals (<15% loss).
Incorrect. Class II features tachycardia but NORMAL systolic blood pressure.
Correct. Class III shock features marked tachycardia, frank hypotension, and confusion (30-40% blood loss).
Incorrect. Class IV features severe collapse with loss of consciousness and >40% loss.
items.kp: Class III hemorrhagic shock (30-40% loss) is characterized by tachycardia >120 and overt hypotension.

items.q: A 42-year-old patient undergoes an urgent laparotomy for a perforated anterior peptic ulcer. Where in the gastrointestinal tract is this perforation most commonly situated?
items.exp: Over 90% of duodenal ulcers occur in the first part of the duodenum (duodenal bulb). Anterior wall ulcers perforate into the peritoneal cavity causing pneumoperitoneum.
r: Correct. The duodenal bulb (D1) is the most frequent site of peptic ulcers and anterior perforation.
Incorrect. D3 is rarely affected by primary peptic ulcer disease.
Incorrect. Gastric fundus ulcers are uncommon compared to antral and duodenal bulb lesions.
Incorrect. D2 ulcers are much less common.
items.kp: The first part of the duodenum (duodenal bulb) is the predominant site for peptic ulcers, with anterior ulcers perforating into the peritoneum.

items.q: In what chemical form is the vast majority (approximately 70-80%) of carbon dioxide transported from peripheral tissues to the lungs in human blood?
o: Carbaminohemoglobin bound to globin amino groups
Dissolved free carbon dioxide gas in physical solution
Carbonic acid molecules inside red blood cells
items.exp: Approximately 70-80% of CO2 is converted inside red cells by carbonic anhydrase into carbonic acid, which dissociates into protons and bicarbonate; bicarbonate is then exchanged for chloride into plasma via AE1.
r: Correct. Bicarbonate in plasma accounts for 70-80% of CO2 transport.
Incorrect. Carbaminohemoglobin accounts for about 15-20%.
Incorrect. Dissolved gas accounts for only 5-10%.
Incorrect. Carbonic acid is an unstable transient intermediate.
items.kp: The majority of blood carbon dioxide (~70-80%) is transported as plasma bicarbonate, generated inside red cells by carbonic anhydrase and exported by the chloride shift.

items.q: A patient is diagnosed with classic scabies. What is the recommended first-line treatment regimen according to NICE guidelines?
o: Permethrin 5% dermal cream applied to the whole body from neck down, left for 8-12 hours, repeated after 7 days, with simultaneous treatment of all household contacts
Oral ivermectin single dose with no contact tracing
Topical hydrocortisone cream applied to itchy spots for 5 days
Permethrin 5% cream applied for 30 minutes once only
items.exp: NICE CKS recommends permethrin 5% dermal cream as first-line therapy. It must be applied to the entire body (from the neck down; including head and neck in infants, elderly or immunocompromised), left on for 8-12 hours before washing off, and repeated after 7 days to kill mites hatched from eggs. All household and sexual contacts must be treated simultaneously regardless of symptoms.
r: Correct: Permethrin 5% cream applied for 8-12 hours, repeated at 7 days, with simultaneous contact treatment.
Contact tracing is mandatory to prevent cyclical reinfection.
Hydrocortisone suppresses itch without killing mites, worsening infestation.
Applying for only 30 minutes is subtherapeutic and fails to eradicate mites.
items.kp: Treat scabies with permethrin 5% cream for 8-12 hours, repeat in 7 days, and treat all contacts simultaneously.

items.q: A 48-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis on methotrexate presents with a red, painful right eye with photophobia and deep boring ocular pain that wakes her from sleep. Visual acuity is normal, but the sclera shows violaceous injection that does not blanch with topical phenylephrine. What is the diagnosis?
items.exp: Scleritis presents with severe, deep boring ocular pain waking the patient from sleep, radiating to the temple, and deep violaceous scleral injection that does not blanch with topical 2.5% phenylephrine (which blanches superficial episcleral vessels in episcleritis). Scleritis carries high risk of globe perforation and demands urgent ophthalmology referral.
r: Correct: Scleritis causes deep nocturnal boring pain and does not blanch with phenylephrine.
Episcleritis is mild or asymptomatic, causes pinkish injection and blanches completely with phenylephrine.
Conjunctivitis causes superficial discharge and grittiness without severe deep pain.
Subconjunctival haemorrhage is painless and flat bright red.
items.kp: Scleritis causes severe deep boring nocturnal pain and fails to blanch with topical phenylephrine.

items.q: An endometrial biopsy in a 54-year-old woman with AUB demonstrates atypical endometrial hyperplasia (endometrial intraepithelial neoplasia). What is the concurrent risk of co-existing invasive endometrial adenocarcinoma on definitive hysterectomy?
items.exp: Multiple landmark prospective Gynecologic Oncology Group (GOG) studies have established that approximately 40% (range 35-43%) of women with a preoperative biopsy diagnosis of atypical endometrial hyperplasia are found to have concurrent invasive endometrial adenocarcinoma upon hysterectomy.
r: Correct. Approximately 40% of patients with atypical hyperplasia harbor concurrent invasive carcinoma.
Incorrect. 2% corresponds to non-atypical simple hyperplasia.
Incorrect. 10% significantly underestimates the risk confirmed by GOG trials.
Incorrect. 90% is overly high.
items.kp: Atypical endometrial hyperplasia carries an approximately 40% concurrent risk of invasive adenocarcinoma on final surgical pathology.

items.q: A 52-year-old woman taking lithium carbonate for bipolar disorder for the past 12 years attends her routine annual check-up. She complains of progressive cold intolerance, dry skin, fatigue, and modest weight gain. Laboratory results show: TSH 14.5 mU/L (normal 0.4-4.0), free T4 7.2 pmol/L (normal 9.0-25.0). Serum lithium is 0.72 mmol/L. What is the diagnosis and recommended clinical management?
o: Lithium-induced primary hypothyroidism; initiate oral levothyroxine replacement and continue lithium if clinically indicated
Immediate discontinuation of lithium with no endocrine replacement
Myxoedema coma; immediate intravenous liothyronine and hydrocortisone in ICU
items.exp: Lithium concentrates in the thyroid gland and inhibits thyroid hormone synthesis and release, causing hypothyroidism in up to 20% of long-term users. The recommended management is to continue lithium (if effective for mood stabilization) and initiate oral levothyroxine replacement, titrating to normalize TSH.
r: Correct: Initiate levothyroxine replacement while continuing lithium if clinically indicated.
Discontinuing lithium abruptly triggers severe bipolar relapse and does not rapidly reverse established hypothyroidism.
Haemodialysis is indicated for life-threatening lithium toxicity (>4.0 mmol/L or severe neurological signs), not a therapeutic level of 0.72.
The patient is ambulatory with mild symptoms, not in myxoedema coma.
items.kp: Lithium-induced hypothyroidism is treated by initiating levothyroxine replacement while continuing lithium therapy.

items.q: A 38-year-old woman undergoes fine-needle aspiration of an asymptomatic 1.8 cm solid hypoechoic thyroid nodule. The cytopathology report states Bethesda Category IV: Follicular Neoplasm. What is the most appropriate next management step?
o: Repeat ultrasound in 12 months without surgery
items.exp: Bethesda Category IV carries a 25% to 40% risk of malignancy. FNA cytology cannot distinguish follicular thyroid adenoma from follicular carcinoma because the diagnosis of malignancy requires histological demonstration of capsular or vascular invasion on permanent sections. Diagnostic lobectomy (or molecular testing) is the established standard of care.
r: Incorrect. Observation alone is inappropriate given the 25-40% malignancy risk.
Correct. Diagnostic thyroid lobectomy provides histological tissue to assess for capsular or vascular invasion.
Incorrect. Radioactive iodine is only used postoperatively for confirmed high-risk thyroid cancer.
Incorrect. External beam radiation is not indicated for follicular neoplasms.
items.kp: Bethesda IV (follicular neoplasm) requires diagnostic lobectomy to assess for capsular or vascular invasion.

items.q: What percentage of total hepatic blood flow is normally delivered by the hepatic portal vein?
items.exp: The portal vein delivers approximately 75% of blood flow to the liver (rich in nutrients from the GI tract), while the hepatic artery delivers the remaining 25% (high in oxygen).
r: Correct. The portal vein supplies approximately 75% of hepatic blood volume.
Incorrect. Hepatic artery provides about 25% of flow.
Incorrect. Flow is not equally split.
Incorrect. Arterial perfusion is mandatory for biliary epithelium.
items.kp: The portal vein supplies roughly 75% of hepatic blood flow, while the hepatic artery supplies the remaining 25%.

items.q: A chronic alcoholic presents with acute confusion, bilateral sixth nerve palsies, and ataxia. Administration of intravenous thiamine improves the ophthalmoplegia. What erythrocyte assay confirms thiamine deficiency?
o: Erythrocyte transketolase activity increase upon adding TPP
Erythrocyte glutathione reductase activation by FAD
items.exp: Thiamine deficiency is diagnostically confirmed by measuring erythrocyte transketolase activity before and after adding thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP). An activity increase >15-25% confirms deficiency.
r: Correct. Erythrocyte transketolase activation by TPP is the diagnostic gold standard.
Incorrect. Glutathione reductase activation by FAD tests for riboflavin (B2) deficiency.
Incorrect. Methylmalonic acid tests for vitamin B12 deficiency.
Incorrect. Transaminases test for B6 or liver injury.
items.kp: Erythrocyte transketolase activity stimulated by exogenous thiamine pyrophosphate confirms thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency.

items.q: A mother brings her 7-year-old daughter to the GP following a school outbreak of head lice. Examination confirms live lice on wet combing. What is the recommended first-line chemical-free physical or physical-insecticide approach in the UK?
o: Dimeticone 4% lotion (or wet combing with fine-toothed nit comb)
items.exp: NICE CKS recommends dimeticone 4% lotion (a physical agent that coats and suffocates lice, to which resistance cannot develop) or systematic wet combing ('bug busting') with a fine-toothed detector comb on wet, conditioned hair. Malathion or dimeticone is applied twice, 7 days apart.
r: Correct: Dimeticone 4% lotion or wet combing is first-line for head lice.
Oral ivermectin is reserved for treatment-resistant outbreaks under specialist advice.
Shaving the scalp causes psychological distress and is unnecessary.
Short-contact permethrin shampoos have high resistance rates and are no longer first-line.
items.kp: Dimeticone 4% lotion or regular wet combing is first-line management for head lice.

items.q: A 48-year-old man presents with recurrent epistaxis, chronic sinusitis, saddle nose deformity, cough with haemoptysis, and rapidly rising serum creatinine. Urinalysis reveals 3+ blood and red cell casts. Which autoantibody is most characteristic of this condition?
items.exp: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA) classically presents with upper airway destruction (recurrent sinusitis, saddle nose), pulmonary involvement (nodules, haemoptysis) and glomerulonephritis, strongly associated with c-ANCA (anti-PR3) antibodies (>90% of active cases).
r: Correct: c-ANCA (anti-PR3) is the diagnostic hallmark of granulomatosis with polyangiitis.
p-ANCA (anti-MPO) is characteristic of microscopic polyangiitis and EGPA.
Anti-GBM antibody causes Goodpasture disease (pulmonary-renal syndrome without upper respiratory tract disease).
Anti-centromere antibody is specific for limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis.
items.kp: c-ANCA (anti-PR3) is the serological hallmark of granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA).

items.q: A 16-year-old girl presents with severe menorrhagia since menarche, requiring blood transfusion. She reports frequent epistaxis and easy bruising. Her mother had severe postpartum bleeding. What is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
items.exp: Severe menorrhagia starting at menarche associated with personal or family history of mucosal bleeding (epistaxis, bruising, postpartum hemorrhage) is the classic presentation of an inherited bleeding disorder, most commonly von Willebrand disease (AUB-C in PALM-COEIN). Up to 20% of adolescents hospitalized for severe AUB have an underlying coagulopathy.
r: Correct. von Willebrand disease is the most common inherited bleeding disorder causing severe menorrhagia at menarche.
Incorrect. ITP causes isolated thrombocytopenia without positive family history of inherited bleeding.
Incorrect. Factor V Leiden is a thrombophilic mutation causing thrombosis, not bleeding.
Incorrect. PCOS causes anovulatory irregular cycles, but mucosal bleeding and positive family history indicate coagulopathy.
items.kp: Severe menorrhagia at menarche with a history of mucosal bleeding strongly indicates von Willebrand disease (AUB-C).

items.q: A 75-year-old man with newly diagnosed dementia with Lewy bodies is admitted to an acute medical ward with a chest infection. He becomes distressed and agitated at night, believing strangers are in his room. The on-call junior doctor considers administering haloperidol. o: Severe, potentially fatal neuroleptic sensitivity (extreme rigidity, sudden immobility, and autonomic collapse)
Risk of precipitating acute pulmonary haemorrhage
items.exp: Patients with dementia with Lewy bodies have extreme neuroleptic sensitivity (affecting up to 50% of patients). Exposure to typical (first-generation) antipsychotics like haloperidol can trigger catastrophic worsening of parkinsonism, 'lead-pipe' rigidity, prolonged sedation, autonomic collapse, neuroleptic malignant syndrome, and substantially elevated mortality. Haloperidol is strictly contraindicated.

Antipsychotics do not cause acute pulmonary haemorrhage.
Antipsychotics do not cause direct optic nerve atrophy.
Antipsychotics do not cause acute nephrolithiasis.
items.kp: Antipsychotics (especially first-generation agents like haloperidol) are strictly contraindicated in DLB due to severe, fatal neuroleptic sensitivity.

items.exp: A LRINEC score >= 6 raises high suspicion for necrotizing soft-tissue infection, while a score >= 8 confers a positive predictive value exceeding 90%.

items.q: Which motor pathway structure crosses in the caudal medulla oblongata at the pyramidal decussation?
items.exp: At the pyramidal decussation in the caudal medulla, approximately 85% of descending corticospinal fibers cross the midline to form the lateral corticospinal tract in the lateral funiculus of the spinal cord.
r: Correct. Corticospinal fibers cross at the medullary pyramidal decussation.
Incorrect. Spinocerebellar tracts ascend uncrossed or double-crossed.
Incorrect. MLF coordinates vestibular and ocular motor nuclei.
Incorrect. Rubrospinal tract decussates in the midbrain.
items.kp: Eighty-five percent of corticospinal fibers cross at the medullary pyramidal decussation to form the lateral corticospinal tract.

items.q: Which enzyme in erythrocytes utilizes NADH to reduce methemoglobin (Fe3+) back to functional ferrous hemoglobin (Fe2+), maintaining normal methemoglobin below 1%?
items.exp: Cytochrome b5 reductase (diaphorase I) uses NADH generated by glycolysis to reduce cytochrome b5, which non-enzymatically reduces ferric iron (Fe3+) back to ferrous iron (Fe2+), maintaining normal methemoglobin <1%.
r: Correct. NADH-cytochrome b5 reductase is the primary physiological methemoglobin reductase.
Incorrect. G6PD generates NADPH, used by a secondary minor reductase pathway.
Incorrect. Glutathione peroxidase detoxifies peroxides.
Incorrect. Superoxide dismutase dismutates superoxide to H2O2.
items.kp: Erythrocytes use NADH-cytochrome b5 reductase to continuously reduce spontaneously formed methemoglobin back to functional ferrous hemoglobin.

items.q: The findings of a single umbilical artery on examination of the umbilical cord after delivery is
o: Equal in incidence in all races
An indicator of considerably increased incidence of major malformation of the fetus
Equally common in newborns of diabetic and nondiabetic mothers
items.exp: The absence of one umbilical artery occurs in 0.7 to 0.8% of all umbilical cords of singletons, in 2.5% of all abouses, and in approximately 5% of at least one twin. The incidence of a single artery is significantly increased in newborns of diabetic mothers, and it occurs in white infants twice as often as in newborns of black women. The incidence of major fetal malformations when only one artery is identified has been reported to be as high as 18%, and there is an increased incidence of overall fetal mortality. The finding is an indication to offer amniocentesis, cordocentesis, or chorionic villus sampling to study fetal chromosomes, although there is debate about whether this should be done when there is only a truly isolated finding of single umbilical artery.

items.q: A 6-year-old girl with atopic eczema has an acute inflammatory flare affecting her cheeks and eyelids with erythema and excoriation. What potency of topical corticosteroid is recommended for her facial skin?
o: Topical corticosteroids are strictly contraindicated on the face
items.exp: NICE CG57 recommends matching topical corticosteroid potency to anatomical site and severity. The face and flexures have thin stratum corneum and are highly vulnerable to dermal atrophy, telangiectasia and perioral dermatitis; only mild-potency corticosteroids (such as 1% hydrocortisone) should be used on the face, for short courses of 3-5 days.
r: Correct: Mild-potency steroids (hydrocortisone 1%) are recommended for facial eczema.
Very potent steroids on the face cause rapid, severe dermal atrophy, striae and perioral dermatitis.
Potent steroids are inappropriate for delicate facial skin in children.
Topical steroids can be used safely on the face when appropriately matched to mild potency.
items.kp: Only mild-potency corticosteroids (e.g. hydrocortisone 1%) should be used on the face in atopic eczema.

items.q: A 42-year-old man with severe, poorly controlled adult-onset asthma presents with bilateral foot drop (mononeuritis multiplex), palpable purpura, and marked peripheral blood eosinophilia (eosinophil count 4.8 x 10^9/L). Which vasculitic disorder is most likely?
items.exp: The triad of adult-onset asthma, marked peripheral eosinophilia (>1.5 x 10^9/L), and systemic vasculitis presenting as mononeuritis multiplex and palpable purpura is pathognomonic of eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA). p-ANCA is positive in approximately 40-50% of cases.
r: Correct: Asthma, peripheral eosinophilia and mononeuritis multiplex characterize EGPA.
GPA features sinonasal bone erosion and c-ANCA without marked peripheral eosinophilia or asthma.
IgA vasculitis presents with abdominal pain, arthritis, purpura and IgA nephropathy, not asthma.
Classical PAN causes medium-vessel aneurysms and is not associated with asthma or eosinophilia.
items.kp: EGPA presents with severe asthma, peripheral eosinophilia, and systemic vasculitis / mononeuritis multiplex.

items.q: Which diagnostic imaging modality has the highest sensitivity for distinguishing an intracavitary endometrial polyp from a submucosal leiomyoma?
items.exp: Saline infusion sonohysterography (SIS) distends the uterine cavity with sterile saline, allowing high-resolution transvaginal sonographic differentiation between flexible, echogenic endometrial polyps and firm, hypoechoic, myometrium-derived submucosal fibroids with over 95% sensitivity.
r: Correct. Saline infusion sonohysterography accurately delineates intracavitary contour and base of attachment.
Incorrect. Transabdominal ultrasound has poor resolution for small intracavitary lesions.
Incorrect. Pelvic CT has poor soft tissue resolution for endometrial intracavitary architecture.
Incorrect. HSG identifies filling defects but cannot distinguish polyp tissue from fibroid tissue.
items.kp: Saline infusion sonohysterography (SIS) is the investigation of choice for distinguishing endometrial polyps from submucosal fibroids.

items.q: A 68-year-old man is brought to the clinic by his spouse, who reports that over the past two years he has been violently acting out vivid nightmares in his sleep, punching the air, kicking, and shouting obscenities, causing bruises to both himself and his wife. Polysomnography demonstrates complete loss of normal motor atonia during REM sleep. What parasomnia is this, and which group of neurodegen
o: REM sleep behaviour disorder (RBD); strongly predicts alpha-synucleinopathies (Parkinson disease, dementia with Lewy bodies, MSA)
NREM sleepwalking; strongly predicts Alzheimer disease
Night terror disorder; strongly predicts Huntington disease
Sleep-related groaning (catathrenia); strongly predicts motor neurone disease
items.exp: REM sleep behaviour disorder (RBD) is characterized by dream-enacting behaviours (punching, kicking, flailing) resulting from loss of the normal physiological motor atonia that characterizes REM sleep. Over 80% of patients with idiopathic RBD convert to an alpha-synucleinopathy (Parkinson disease, dementia with Lewy bodies, or multiple system atrophy) within 10 to 15 years.
r: Correct: REM sleep behaviour disorder is characterized by dream enactment without REM atonia and strongly predicts alpha-synucleinopathies.
Sleepwalking occurs during NREM slow-wave sleep and does not predict Alzheimer disease.
Night terrors are NREM parasomnias occurring in deep sleep and do not predict Huntington disease.
Catathrenia is benign nocturnal groaning with no link to MND.
items.kp: REM sleep behaviour disorder involves dream-enacting behaviors due to loss of REM atonia and is a major prodromal marker for alpha-synucleinopathies.

items.q: Which of the following operative wound classes carries the highest baseline risk of postoperative surgical site infection without prophylaxis?
items.exp: Class IV (Dirty/Infected) wounds involve existing clinical infection or perforated viscera, carrying infection rates exceeding 30-40%.
r: Correct. Class IV (Dirty/Infected) wounds involve existing clinical infection or perforated viscera

items.q: A post-splenectomy patient is at lifelong risk for overwhelming postsplenectomy infection (OPSI). Which encapsulated bacterium is the most common cause of fatal post-splenectomy sepsis?
items.exp: Streptococcus pneumoniae accounts for over 50-70% of all cases of overwhelming post-splenectomy sepsis, followed by Neisseria meningitidis and Haemophilus influenzae.
r: Correct. Streptococcus pneumoniae is the leading culprit in overwhelming post-splenectomy infection.
Incorrect. E. coli is not an encapsulated organism relying primarily on splenic opsonin clearance.
Incorrect. Pseudomonas causes opportunistic hospital-acquired infections.
Incorrect. Staph aureus causes soft tissue and catheter sepsis.
items.kp: Streptococcus pneumoniae is the most frequent and lethal pathogen in overwhelming postsplenectomy infection (OPSI).

items.q: During prolonged fasting (>48 hours), which organ becomes an important secondary contributor to systemic gluconeogenesis, producing up to 40-50% of circulating glucose?
items.exp: While the liver provides nearly all glucose during early fasting, during prolonged starvation the renal cortex upregulates gluconeogenesis (using glutamine as primary substrate), supplying up to 40-50% of circulating glucose.
r: Correct. Renal cortex contributes up to 40-50% of gluconeogenesis during prolonged starvation.
Incorrect. Muscle lacks glucose-6-phosphatase and cannot export glucose.
Incorrect. Adipose tissue lacks gluconeogenic enzymes.
Incorrect. Small intestine absorbs nutrients but is a minor glucose producer.
items.kp: During prolonged starvation, renal cortical gluconeogenesis increases substantially, providing nearly half of circulating endogenous glucose using glutamine.

items.q: A 32-year-old woman with severe atopic eczema requires frequent courses of potent topical steroids on her eyelids and neck, leading to cutaneous atrophy and striae. Which topical non-steroidal immunomodulator is licensed and recommended as a steroid-sparing agent for delicate sites?
items.exp: Topical calcineurin inhibitors (tacrolimus 0.03% and 0.1% ointment, and pimecrolimus cream) are licensed second-line treatments for atopic eczema. Because they do not inhibit collagen synthesis, they do not cause skin atrophy, telangiectasia or striae, making them ideal steroid-sparing agents for the face, eyelids, and neck.
r: Correct: Topical tacrolimus is a calcineurin inhibitor that spares steroid atrophy on the face and neck.
Fluorouracil is a cytotoxic antimetabolite for actinic keratoses and basal cell carcinoma.
Imiquimod is an immune response modifier for warts and superficial BCC.
Podophyllotoxin is an antimitotic for anogenital warts.
items.kp: Topical calcineurin inhibitors (tacrolimus) provide steroid-sparing therapy without causing cutaneous atrophy.

items.q: A 32-year-old man with ankylosing spondylitis presents to eye casualty with a 24-hour history of acute left eye pain, redness, photophobia and blurred vision. Examination reveals ciliary injection, cells in the anterior chamber and an irregular pupil. What is the diagnosis?
items.exp: Acute anterior uveitis (iritis) is the most frequent extra-articular manifestation of axial spondyloarthritis, occurring in 25-40% of patients. It presents acutely with unilateral eye pain, redness, photophobia, ciliary flush and miosis. Urgent treatment with topical corticosteroids and mydriatics is required to prevent posterior synechiae.
r: Correct: Acute anterior uveitis causes unilateral painful red eye with photophobia and anterior chamber cells.
Bacterial keratitis features a visible corneal infiltrate and epithelial defect on fluorescein staining.
Acute angle-closure glaucoma causes a fixed mid-dilated pupil, corneal haziness and marked intraocular pressure rise.
Episcleritis is mildly painful, causes localized sectorial injection, and lacks anterior chamber cells.
items.kp: Acute anterior uveitis is the commonest extra-articular complication of ankylosing spondylitis.

items.q: What is the recommended initial management for a 50-year-old perimenopausal woman with atypical endometrial hyperplasia who has completed childbearing and is medically fit?
o: Oral high-dose megestrol acetate for 6 months
Insertion of 52 mg LNG-IUS with observation

Progestin therapy is reserved strictly for patients desiring fertility preservation or unfit for surgery.
r: Correct. Hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy is the standard definitive treatment.
Incorrect. Medical progestin therapy is second-line, reserved only for fertility preservation or high surgical risk.
Incorrect. Endometrial ablation is contraindicated because it prevents future histological surveillance and can trap cancer.
Incorrect. LNG-IUS alone is not first-line when childbearing is complete and patient is surgical candidate.
items.kp: Total hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy is the definitive treatment for atypical endometrial hyperplasia.

items.q: What is the recommended surgical margin for complete excision of a low-risk, well-demarcated basal cell carcinoma smaller than 2 cm on the trunk?

items.q: In which anatomical zone of the prostate gland do approximately 75% of prostate adenocarcinomas arise?
items.exp: The peripheral zone forms approximately 70% of the volume of the prostate gland and accounts for 75% of prostatic adenocarcinomas, which are easily palpated on digital rectal examination.
r: Correct. Peripheral zone is the primary site of origin for prostatic adenocarcinoma.
Incorrect. Transition zone is where benign prostatic hyperplasia originates.
Incorrect. Central zone surrounds the ejaculatory ducts and rarely develops carcinoma.

items.kp: Seventy-five percent of prostate adenocarcinomas originate in the peripheral zone, palpated via digital rectal exam.

items.q: A female infant presents on day 10 of life with ambiguous genitalia, severe dehydration, hyponatremia, and hyperkalemia. Plasma 17-hydroxyprogesterone is markedly elevated. Which enzyme is deficient?
items.exp: 21-hydroxylase deficiency accounts for >90% of congenital adrenal hyperplasia. Failure to convert 17-OHP to 11-deoxycortisol causes cortisol and aldosterone deficiency (salt wasting, shock) and shunts precursors into androgens (virilization).
r: Correct. 21-hydroxylase deficiency causes salt-wasting CAH with elevated 17-OHP and virilization.
Incorrect. 11-beta-hydroxylase deficiency accumulates 11-DOC, causing hypertension, not salt wasting.
Incorrect. 17-alpha-hydroxylase deficiency causes hypokalemia, hypertension, and feminization.
Incorrect. 3-beta-HSD deficiency causes elevated DHEA.
items.kp: 21-hydroxylase (CYP21A2) deficiency is the most common CAH, presenting with salt-wasting crisis (hyponatremia, hyperkalemia) and ambiguous genitalia due to accumulated 17-hydroxyprogesterone shunted into androgens.

items.q: A 38-year-old man with plaque psoriasis presents with painful swelling of the distal interphalangeal (DIP) joints of his hands and whole-digit swelling ('sausage digit'). Inspection of his fingernails shows punctate pitting, subungual hyperkeratosis, and yellow-brown 'salmon patch' oil drop discoloration. What is the diagnosis?
items.exp: Nail changes (pitting, oil drop discoloration, onycholysis, subungual hyperkeratosis) occur in up to 80% of patients with psoriatic arthritis and correlate closely with distal interphalangeal (DIP) joint inflammation and dactylitis ('sausage digit').
r: Correct: Nail pitting, salmon patches, DIP arthritis, and dactylitis define psoriatic arthritis.
Rheumatoid arthritis classically spares DIP joints, does not cause salmon oil-drop nail patches, and is symmetric.
Osteoarthritis causes Heberden nodes without dactylitis, silvery skin plaques, or salmon oil patches.
Gout typically causes acute monoarthritis of the first MTP joint with urate crystal deposition.
items.kp: Psoriatic nail changes (pitting, salmon patches) are strongly associated with psoriatic arthritis and DIP involvement.

items.q: A 55-year-old man with ankylosing spondylitis presents with progressive dyspnoea on exertion and a high-pitched early diastolic murmur heard best at the left sternal edge on expiration. Echocardiography shows severe aortic regurgitation with aortic root dilation. What is the pathological mechanism?
o: Aortitis and root dilation associated with ankylosing spondylitis
items.exp: Aortitis and fibrous thickening of the aortic root and valve cusps occur in up to 5-10% of patients with chronic ankylosing spondylitis, resulting in aortic root dilatation, cusp retraction and progressive aortic regurgitation.

Infective endocarditis features fever, positive blood cultures and mobile vegetations.
Rheumatic disease causes cusp fusion and mitral stenosis.
Calcific aortic stenosis produces a systolic ejection murmur, not diastolic regurgitation.
items.kp: Aortic root dilatation and aortic regurgitation are recognized cardiac complications of chronic ankylosing spondylitis.

items.q: According to the World Health Organization (WHO 2021, 6th edition) laboratory manual, what is the lower reference limit for total sperm motility in a normal semen analysis?
items.exp: Under the WHO 2021 (6th edition) semen analysis manual guidelines, the fifth percentile lower reference limits are: semen volume 1.4 mL, sperm concentration 16 million/mL, total motility 42% (or progressive motility 30%), and normal forms 4.0%.

Incorrect. 60% exceeds the standard 5th percentile reference cutoff.
Incorrect. 25% represents significant asthenozoospermia.
Incorrect. 15% reflects severe motility impairment.
items.kp: WHO 2021 semen analysis lower reference limits require >= 42% total motility (>= 30% progressive motility) and >= 4% normal forms.

items.q: A neonate with hypotonia and poor feeding develops compulsive hyperphagia and obesity in childhood. Genetic testing confirms Prader-Willi syndrome. What is the genetic mechanism?
o: Loss of paternal 15q11-q13 expression (deletion or maternal UPD)
Loss of maternal 15q11-q13 expression (deletion or paternal UPD)
Trinucleotide CGG repeat expansion in FMR1
items.exp: Prader-Willi syndrome results from absent expression of paternally derived genes on 15q11-q13, due to paternal deletion (70%) or maternal uniparental disomy (25%).
r: Correct. Prader-Willi syndrome results from absent expression of paternally derived genes on 15q11-q13, due to paternal deletion (70%) or maternal uniparental disomy (25%).
Incorrect. Loss of maternal 15q11-q13 expression (deletion or paternal UPD) does not explain the primary biochemical mechanism described.
Incorrect. Trinucleotide CGG repeat expansion in FMR1 does not explain the primary biochemical mechanism described.

items.kp: Prader-Willi syndrome results from absent paternal 15q11-q13 gene expression, causing neonatal hypotonia followed by severe hyperphagia.

items.q: A 62-year-old man with rigid 'bamboo spine' from advanced ankylosing spondylitis sustains a low-energy fall from a standing position. He complains of acute neck pain. Neurological examination is currently intact. What is the mandatory immediate radiological investigation?
items.exp: A rigid, fused spine acts as a long bone; minor low-energy trauma can cause unstable 'chalk-stick' fractures with high risk of spinal cord transection and epidural haematoma. Discharging without CT risks delayed displacement and catastrophic quadriplegia.
Plain radiographs miss many fractures due to osteopenia and distorted anatomy.
Flexion-extension views are dangerous and strictly contraindicated in acute trauma.
items.kp: Low-energy falls in ankylosing spondylitis require urgent CT imaging to exclude unstable chalk-stick fractures.

items.q: A hysterosalpingogram (HSG) in a 32-year-old infertile woman demonstrates bilateral dilated fallopian tubes with a retort-shaped appearance and absence of free peritoneal contrast spill. What is the diagnosis?
o: Tubal spasm at the uterotubal junction
items.exp: A dilated, fluid-filled, retort-shaped fallopian tube with failure of peritoneal contrast spill is characteristic of hydrosalpinx, typically resulting from distal fimbrial occlusion secondary to prior pelvic inflammatory disease. Hydrosalpinges contain toxic fluid that reduces IVF implantation by 50% unless clipped or removed.

items.kp: Hydrosalpinx presents on HSG as distal tubal ballooning without peritoneal spill and should be removed before IVF.

items.q: In the lateral nasal wall cross-section, where does the nasolacrimal duct terminate and drain?

The middle meatus receives the frontal, maxillary, and anterior ethmoidal sinuses; the superior meatus receives posterior ethmoidal air cells; and the sphenoethmoidal recess receives the sphenoid sinus.

Incorrect. Posterior ethmoidal air cells drain into superior meatus.
Incorrect. Frontal and maxillary sinuses drain into middle meatus.
Correct. The nasolacrimal duct drains into the inferior meatus under the valve of Hasner.
items.kp: Nasolacrimal duct drains into the inferior meatus beneath the inferior concha.

items.q: A 30-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis well-controlled on methotrexate and sulfasalazine announces she is planning pregnancy with her partner in four months. What is the most appropriate management regarding her DMARDs?
o: Stop methotrexate immediately and switch to pregnancy-compatible therapy such as certolizumab pegol
Continue methotrexate throughout pregnancy at reduced dose
Stop all medications and permit unmonitored disease flare
items.exp: Methotrexate is teratogenic and embryotoxic; BSR guidelines recommend stopping methotrexate at least three months prior to conception. Certolizumab pegol (a pegylated Fab fragment without an Fc domain) does not cross the placenta and is safe throughout pregnancy; sulfasalazine is also compatible with pregnancy when co-prescribed with 5 mg daily folic acid.

items.q: Which of the following conditions represents an absolute contraindication to systemic hormone replacement therapy?
o: Active or past history of breast cancer

items.q: From what cm of cervical dilatation is partogram plotted in regular intervals?
items.exp: The best method to monitor labour is through the partograph ! The partograph is a graphic record of the progress of labour and relevant details of the mother and fetus The WHO partograph begins only in the active phase of labour, when the cervix is 4 cm or more dilated Observations to be made: Maternal well - being: Pulse every 30 minutes Blood pressure and temperature 4-hourly Urine output and dipstick testing for protein Ketones (if available) and glucose after vooding Fetal well - being: Record fetal heart rate for 1 minute every 15-30 minutes after a contraction in the first stage Every 5 minutes in the second stage If abnormalities are noted, urgent delivery can be considered. Liquor: Clear Meconium stained (thick or thin) Bloody Absent Thick meconium suggests fetal distress Moulding 0= bones are separated and sutures can be easily felt; +1 = bones are just touching each other; +2 = bones are overlapping but can be reduced; +3 = bones are severely overlapping and irreducible. Cervical dilatation:assess at each VAGINAL EXAMINATION and mark with a cross x. Begin at 4 cm. Alert line: starting at 4 cm of cervical dilatation, up to the point of expected full dilatation at the rate of 1 cm per hour. Action line: parallel and 4 hours to the right of the alert line. Descent of head:assessed by abdominal palpation: this refers to the part of the head (which is divided into five parts) palpable above the symphysis pubis;recorded as a circle (O)at every vaginal examination. At 0/5, the sinciput (S) is at the level of the symphysis pubis. PLEASE NOTE: Newer guidelines are now suggesting onset of active labour and thus initial marking to be plotted at 6 cm dilatation. However till consensus is achieved on this, the previous definition of 4 cm shall be accepted for answering. Students should be on the lookout for such a guideline.

The condition occurs in known viral infections (herpes zoster, Epstein-Barr virus), following injections of tetanus toxoid, in putative viral infections; and as an autobnmune disorder following a surgical procedure."- Basic neurology By John Gilroy 3/e p594 Brachial plexus neuritis usually is characterized by the acute onset of excruciating unilateral shoulder pain, followed by flaccid paralysis of shoulder and parascapular muscles several days later. items.q: Which of the following is preferred treatment after birth for baby of HBsAg positive mother?
items.exp: Hep B immunoglobulin + Hep B immunization o Hepatitis B virus (HBV): It is a global public health problem. The virus is transmitted by parenteral route, sexual contact, vertical transmission and rarely through breast milk. Approximately 25% of the carrier neonate will die from cirrhosis or hepatic carcinoma, between late childhood to early adulthood. HBV is not teratogenic.Recommended treatment for infants born to HBsAg positive mother:o Infants bom to HBsAg-positive mothers should receive HBIG (0.5 mL) intramuscularly (IM) once they are physiologically stable, preferably within 12 hours after birtho HB vaccine, either plasma-derived (10 *gmg per dose) or recombinant (5 *gmg per dose), should be administered IM in three doses of 0.5 mL each.o The first dose should be given concurrently with HBIG but at a different site. If vaccine is not immediately available, the first dose can be given within 7 days after birth. The second and third doses should be given 1 month and 6 months after the first.o Testing the infant for HBsAg and its antibody (anti-HBs) is recommended at 12-15 months of age to monitor the effectiveness of therapy. If HBsAg is not detectable and anti-HBs is present, the child can be considered protected. Testing for antibody to hepatitis B core antigen (anti-HBc) is not useful, since maternal anti-HBc can persist for more than a year.o HBIG and HB vaccination do not interfere with the routine childhood immunizations.
